sections.title: 1. Core Study Notes
sections.content:
Detailed study guide and resources for Economy are currently being prepared. Check back soon for comprehensive explanations, summary diagrams, and expert preparation recommendations.

Key Dimensions of Study:

  • Definition, scope, and foundational theories.
  • Relevance to General Studies Paper & Contemporary contexts.
  • Core applications and structural framework.

practiceQuestions.q: During the Delhi Sultanate, what was the term used for the revenue-free land granted to religious leaders and scholars?
practiceQuestions.sol: In the Delhi Sultanate, land grants given to religious persons, scholars, and the poor were often termed 'Inam' or 'Wakf' (while 'Madad-i-Maash' or 'Suyurghal' was the prominent Mughal equivalent, the Delhi Sultanate used terms like Inam and Milk). Khalisa refers to crown lands. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 7 & 11 History / Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: Which Mughal emperor introduced the Dahshahas (or Zabt) system of land revenue administration?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Dahshahas system, an evolution of the Zabt system, was introduced by Raja Todar Mal under Emperor Akbar in 1580. It calculated revenue based on the average yield of crops and prices prevailing over the preceding 10 years. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II]

practiceQuestions.q: What does the term 'Iqta' signify in the context of the Delhi Sultanate?
opts: A revenue-yielding territorial unit assigned to a noble
A royal mint for minting gold coins
practiceQuestions.sol: An 'Iqta' was a revenue-yielding territorial assignment given by the Sultans of Delhi to nobles, officers, and military commanders (Iqtadars or Muqtis) in lieu of cash salaries. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 History / Satish Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q: During medieval India, the term 'Jizya' was primarily which type of tax?
opts: Religious tax levied on non-Muslim subjects
practiceQuestions.sol: Jizya was a mandatory per capita tax levied by Islamic states on non-Muslim subjects (zimmis) living within Muslim lands, in exchange for protection and exemption from military service. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 7 & 12 History]

practiceQuestions.q: What was 'Tanka' and 'Jital' during the reign of Iltutmish?
practiceQuestions.sol: Iltutmish was the first sultan to reform the currency system of the Delhi Sultanate. He introduced the silver Tanka and copper Jital as standard coins, giving economic stability to the nascent empire. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: Under the Vijayanagara Empire, what were the 'Ayyagars'?
opts: Hereditary village functionaries governing rural administration
High-ranking cavalry commanders in the royal army
Overseas merchant guilds trading in spices
practiceQuestions.sol: The Ayyagars were a group of 12 hereditary village functionaries in the Vijayanagara Empire who managed village affairs, local production, and revenue collection. [Primary Reference: NCERT History / Epigraphical studies of South India]

practiceQuestions.q: What did the term 'Sarraf' or 'Shroff' signify in the medieval Indian economy?
opts: Money changer, banker, and bill-of-exchange (Hundi) specialist
practiceQuestions.sol: Sarafs or Shroffs acted as indigenous bankers and money changers in medieval India. They evaluated the purity of coins, issued and discounted hundis (bills of exchange), and facilitated long-distance trade. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q: What was a 'Hundi' in the context of medieval Indian commerce?
opts: A heavy iron cannon used in sieges
A financial instrument acting as a bill of exchange or credit note
An annual tax paid by nomadic pastoralists
A type of cargo boat used on river routes
practiceQuestions.sol: A Hundi was a financial instrument developed in medieval India used in trade and credit transactions. It functioned as a bill of exchange or promissory note, enabling merchants to transfer money across regions safely without physical transportation of cash. [Primary Reference: NCERT Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: Under the Mughal administration, what was 'Polaj' land?
opts: Land left uncultivated for 3 to 4 years to regain fertility
Land that was annually cultivated for every harvest without break
Barren rocky land completely unfit for agriculture
Land flooded by rivers during monsoon season
practiceQuestions.sol: Under Akbar's revenue classification, 'Polaj' was the best category of land that was cultivated continuously year after year and never allowed to lie fallow. [Primary Reference: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari]

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following terms denoted the state's share of agricultural produce during the Sultanate and Mughal periods?
practiceQuestions.sol: Kharaj was the land tax levied on agricultural produce of non-Muslims (and later generalized) under Islamic law and the Delhi Sultanate/Mughal administration, often constituting one-third to one-half of the produce. [Primary Reference: NCERT Medieval India History]

practiceQuestions.q: How did Alauddin Khalji's market control policy fundamentally alter the military and economic structure of the Delhi Sultanate?
opts: It encouraged laissez-faire trade, allowing merchants to charge market-determined prices for maximum profits.
It fixed the prices of essential commodities so that a large standing army could be maintained economically on low salaries.
It abolished all cash transactions and enforced a pure barter economy throughout North India.
It privatized grain storage facilities to eliminate state involvement in food security.
practiceQuestions.sol: Alauddin Khalji needed to maintain a massive standing army to repel Mongol invasions and expand his empire, but treasury constraints prevented high cash salaries. By strictly fixing grain, cloth, and slave prices, he ensured soldiers could live comfortably on modest pay. [Primary Reference: Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi / NCERT History]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the structural difference between the 'Jagir' system of the Mughals and the 'Iqta' system of the Delhi Sultanate?
opts: Iqtas were strictly hereditary land properties, whereas Jagirs were non-transferable temporary assignments.
Jagirs were part of the centralized Mansabdari system with frequent transfers to prevent localized power, whereas early Iqtas tended to become more hereditary and feudal over time.
Jagirs generated revenue exclusively from foreign trade, whereas Iqtas relied only on agricultural tax.
There was no administrative difference; 'Jagir' is simply a Persian word for the exact same institution.
Jagirs generated revenue exclusively from foreign trade, whereas Iqtas relied only on agricultural tax.
practiceQuestions.sol: While both involved revenue assignments, the Mughal Jagirdari system was deeply integrated with the bureaucratic Mansabdari network, where jagirdars were frequently transferred every 3-4 years to curb autonomous power bases. Early Delhi Sultanate Iqtas often functioned with greater regional autonomy and vulnerability to hereditary consolidation. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India / Irfan Habib]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the 'Mansabdari system' introduced by Akbar impact the agrarian economy and military administration?
opts: It converted all agricultural land into private zamindari estates exempt from royal audit.
It established a hierarchical grading of imperial officers (Mansabdars) who were assigned revenues (Jagirs) to maintain specific military contingents.
It eliminated the cash-crop economy in favor of forced subsistence paddy farming.
It banned the use of minted currency and mandated barter trade for all military supplies.
practiceQuestions.sol: The Mansabdari system was a unique military-civil administrative apparatus where every officer was assigned a rank (Mansab) indicating their status and the number of horsemen (Zat and Sawar) they must maintain. Their salary was paid via revenue assignments (Jagirs). [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 12 History]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the economic significance of the 'Nayankara system' in the Vijayanagara Empire?
opts: It was a central banking mechanism controlling international maritime trade tariffs.
It granted military chiefs (Nayaks) administrative control over territories in exchange for maintaining troops and paying a fixed annual financial tribute to the king.
It abolished the caste system to create an egalitarian labor force for agrarian expansion.
It was a cooperative guild system formed exclusively by foreign Arab horse traders.
practiceQuestions.sol: The Nayankara system was a core pillar of Vijayanagara's political economy. Military commanders called Nayaks were assigned territory (Amaram) from which they collected revenue to maintain troops and remit a tribute to the central royal treasury. [Primary Reference: Noboru Karashima, South Indian History and Society]

practiceQuestions.q: Why did the medieval Indian economy experience a robust monetization phase during the Mughal era despite being primarily agrarian?
opts: Because the state demanded land revenue compulsorily in cash rather than grain, compelling peasants to sell surplus produce in markets.
Because the discovery of vast paper-currency reserves in Bengal eliminated the need for metallic coins.
Because foreign colonial powers banned all non-monetary economic bartering by imperial decree.
Because the Mughal emperors prohibited agricultural production and converted the entire subcontinent into urban manufacturing hubs.
practiceQuestions.sol: A key feature of the Mughal agrarian economy was the requirement that revenue (Zabt rates) be assessed and paid in cash (Naqd). This forced peasants to enter rural markets to sell their crops for silver rupees and copper dams, deeply integrating the village economy into broader market networks. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the economic function of 'Karkhanas' in the Mughal Empire?
opts: Independent peasant cooperatives that manufactured agricultural tools.
State-run imperial workshops producing luxury items, weapons, and textiles for the royal household and army.
International trading ports established along the Malabar Coast.
Financial clearinghouses operated by indigenous Shroffs for discounting hundis.
practiceQuestions.sol: Karkhanas were state-maintained workshops where skilled artisans (weavers, armorers, goldsmiths, jewelers) worked under imperial supervision to produce luxury goods, imperial regalia, and military equipment. [Primary Reference: Bernier's Travels / Satish Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the influx of American silver into Europe during the 16th and 17th centuries indirectly impact the Indian economy via maritime trade?
opts: It caused a massive economic depression in India due to a collapse in demand for Indian textiles.
European traders brought vast amounts of this bullion to India to purchase textiles and spices, fueling a vibrant bullion-for-goods trade and economic expansion.
It forced Indian rulers to abandon metallic currency and revert entirely to a grain-based barter standard.
It had zero impact because India maintained a completely closed autarkic economic policy.
practiceQuestions.sol: Europeans lacked goods desired by Asians except for precious metals. The massive inflow of New World silver into Europe found its way to Asia, particularly India, as European East India companies purchased Indian cotton textiles and spices with silver bullion. This made India a 'sink of silver' and boosted domestic liquidity. [Primary Reference: Om Prakash, European Commercial Enterprise in Pre-Colonial India]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the role of the 'Mir Jumla' or 'Shah-bandar' in Mughal maritime and coastal trade governance?
opts: They were supreme religious judges overseeing Islamic jurisprudence in rural courts.
Shah-bandar was the chief harbor master and customs official at major ports regulating shipping, port duties, and foreign merchant interactions.
They commanded the imperial artillery regiments during siege warfare.
They were agricultural tax assessors responsible for measuring crop yields in the doab region.
practiceQuestions.sol: The Shah-bandar was the principal official at royal ports (such as Surat), responsible for supervising customs collection, registering shipping, ensuring port security, and dealing with European and Asian merchants. [Primary Reference: Ashin Das Gupta, Indian Merchants and the Decline of Surat]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the emergence of the 'Zamindar' class shape the agrarian relations of the Mughal Empire?
opts: Zamindars were absolute owners of all land with powers to evict peasants at will, functioning as pure feudal lords.
Zamindars held hereditary rights to a share of produce (malikana) or collected revenue on behalf of the state, possessing proprietary ties to land and exercising considerable local dominance.
Zamindars were salaried state bureaucrats appointed directly by the emperor for one-year terms without any local roots.
Zamindars were nomadic pastoralists who paid taxes exclusively in livestock and dairy products.
practiceQuestions.sol: Unlike European feudal lords, Mughal zamindars did not own all the land (peasants had occupancy rights), but zamindars held hereditary claims to a cut of the revenue (malikana) and often controlled proprietary wasteland and armed retainers. They formed a crucial intermediary layer between the imperial administration and the peasantry. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the economic significance of long-distance inland trade routes (Caravan sarais) during the medieval period?
opts: They served exclusively as military outposts for stationing cavalry units against bandits.
They facilitated commerce by providing secure lodging, storage for goods, and communication networks along major imperial highways like the Grand Trunk Road.
They were tax-collection booths established to levy heavy transit duties on pilgrims.
They functioned as royal mints where counterfeit detection experts verified currency purity.
practiceQuestions.sol: Caravan sarais built along major routes (prominently by Sher Shah Suri and the Mughal emperors) provided safe halting places for merchants and travelers, acting as vital nodes for commercial exchange, information dissemination, and safe transit of high-value goods. [Primary Reference: NCERT Medieval Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the agrarian reforms of Alauddin Khalji:
1. He increased the land revenue (Kharaj) to half of the produce in the Doab region.
2. He introduced the system of measurement (Biswa) as the basis of assessment.
3. He abolished all traditional intermediary rights of Khuts, Muqaddams, and Chaudhuris.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: All three statements are correct. Alauddin Khalji raised revenue to 50% in the fertile Doab region, mandated land measurement (Biswa) to assess exact yields, and curbed the privileges of local rural elites (Khuts, Muqaddams, Chaudhuris) by forcing them to pay taxes like ordinary cultivators. [Primary Reference: Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi / Satish Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Sher Shah Suri's economic and administrative reforms:
1. He introduced the fine silver coin known as 'Rupiya', which served as a precursor to the modern rupee.
2. He standardized weights and measures across his empire by introducing the Gaz-i-Sikandari.
3. He reorganized the land revenue system by classifying land into good, middle, and bad categories.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: Sher Shah introduced the silver Rupiya (weighing 178 grains), which became the basis of British and modern Indian currency. Statement 3 is correct: He classified land into Polaj, Parauti, etc., based on fertility (good, middle, bad). Statement 2 is incorrect because the 'Gaz-i-Sikandari' was introduced earlier by Sikandar Lodi (Sher Shah used the Sikandari gaz or Ilahi gaz depending on context, but Sikandari gaz was specifically Lodi's standard). [Primary Reference: Abbas Khan Sarwani, Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi / NCERT]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Mughal agrarian classification of land:
1. Polaj was land that was left fallow for a year or two to recover its lost fertility.
2. Chachar was land kept uncultivated for three to four years.
3. Banjar was barren or wasteland that was uncultivated for five years or more.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect: Polaj was land cultivated annually without interruption; land left fallow for 1-2 years was called 'Parauti'. Statements 2 and 3 are correct: Chachar was fallow for 3-4 years, and Banjar was uncultivated for 5 or more years. [Primary Reference: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari / NCERT Class 12 History]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the financial administration of the Delhi Sultanate:
1. Diwan-i-Wizarat was the department headed by the Wazir, responsible for finance, revenue collection, and expenditure.
2. Diwan-i-Arif was the department of agriculture established by Muhammad bin Tughlaq to provide loans (Takavi) to farmers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: The Wazir headed the Diwan-i-Wizarat, managing the central exchequer and revenue administration. Statement 2 is incorrect: Diwan-i-Arif (or Ariz-i-Mumalik) was the military department, not agriculture. The department of agriculture created by Muhammad bin Tughlaq was called 'Diwan-i-Kohi'. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding foreign trade and commercial items in medieval India:
1. India exported large quantities of cotton textiles, raw silk, and precious gemstones to Europe and West Asia.
2. Horses were among the most critical high-value imports into India, sourced from Central Asia and Arabia.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. India was the industrial workshop of the world, exporting cotton textiles across the globe. Concurrently, because Indian horses were generally of inferior military breed, rulers and merchants imported thousands of warhorses annually from Arabia, Persia, and Central Asia via ports like Surat and Calicut. [Primary Reference: NCERT Themes in Indian History / Irfan Habib]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the revenue assessment systems under Akbar:
1. In the 'Batalai' (crop-sharing) system, the state's share was fixed directly on the standing crop or after threshing.
2. In the 'Zabt' system, revenue was calculated based on cash schedule rates (Dastur-ul-amal) derived from past yield and prices.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are accurate descriptions of Mughal revenue methods. Batalai (or Bhaoli/Ghalibaksh) involved actual division of the crop between state and peasant, while Zabt was a sophisticated cash-assessment system utilizing standardized schedules (dasturs) per crop per unit area. [Primary Reference: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari / Irfan Habib]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the economic features of the Vijayanagara Empire:
1. The empire issued gold coins known as 'Varahas' or 'Pagodas', which were widely circulated in international trade.
2. Foreign travelers like Domingo Paes and Niccolo Conti left glowing accounts of the urban prosperity and bustling markets of Vijayanagara city.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Vijayanagara minted high-purity gold coins called Varahas (or Pagodas), which facilitated extensive commerce. Accounts by Portuguese traveler Domingo Paes, Italian Niccolo Conti, and Persian Abdur Razzaq heavily praised the wealth, market organization, and commercial scale of the capital. [Primary Reference: Robert Sewell, A Forgotten Empire / NCERT]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the 'Jagirdari Crisis' in the late Mughal Empire:
1. It refers to the severe shortage of revenue-yielding jagirs (pai-baksh) relative to the number of claimants (Mansabdars).
2. This crisis led to intensified peasant oppression as jagirdars sought to extract maximum revenue in their short tenures.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct and form the core thesis of Satish Chandra's and Irfan Habib's analysis of the Mughal decline. Expansion of the empire under Aurangzeb increased the number of mansabdars without a proportionate increase in productive crown or assignable lands, causing fierce competition for jagirs and desperate extraction of revenue from peasantry, triggering agrarian rebellions. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Parties and Politics at the Mughal Court]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding agricultural technology and crops introduced in medieval India:
1. New crops like tobacco, maize, and chillies were introduced to India by the Portuguese during the 16th and 17th centuries.
2. Persian wheel (Araghatta) technology was widely adopted during the medieval period to improve artificial irrigation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. The Columbian exchange brought American crops like tobacco, maize, potato, tomato, and chillies via Portuguese traders. Furthermore, the Persian wheel (Araghatta), which utilized gear-wheel mechanisms driven by oxen, transformed well-irrigation in North India during the Sultanate and Mughal eras. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Technology in Medieval India / NCERT]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the role of merchant guilds in medieval South India:
1. Guilds like 'Ainurruvar' (Manigramam and Ayyavole) wielded immense economic power, engaging in extensive domestic and overseas maritime trade.
2. These guilds maintained their own armed militias to protect merchandise trade routes from bandits and warring factions.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Powerful South Indian merchant guilds such as Ayyavole (The Five Hundred) and Manigramam controlled vast trade networks spanning South India, Southeast Asia, and China. Because long-distance trade routes traversed insecure terrains, these corporate merchant bodies maintained their own armed guards (viragodas) for protection. [Primary Reference: K.A. Nilakanta Sastry, A History of South India / Epigraphical Evidence]
